Youth Development Programmes—Young Leaders Auckland Pilot Programme
12. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister for Ethnic Affairs : What is the
Government doing to increase the leadership capabilities in youth of ethnic minorities?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: First off, congratulations,
Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The Office of Ethnic Affairs has launched the Young
Leaders Auckland Pilot Programme. Along with the Ministry of Youth Development, it
is running a 9-month training course for 10 young Aucklanders. These young leaders of
the future will learn crucia l skills such as advocacy, public speaking, and project
management. The participants will enjoy va luable opportunities to learn about how a
Government works, the value of comm unity volunteering, and the importance of
professional networking activities. Of course, they will also learn to be professional,
unlike that lot over there.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: Why is this programme necessa ry for youth of smaller ethnic
communities? [Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Unfortunately, the Labour  Party considers ethnic
minorities something to laugh at, but this Government is committed to a productive and
harmonious New Zealand where ethnic minorities equally feel that they have the ability
and skills to participate. Ill-informed prejudi ces of a select few may also add additional
challenges. It is essential that we equip these young people to become leaders who will
not only make a personal contri bution to civic, economic, and social outcomes but also
pass on their experience and knowledge to their communities.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That brings to an end oral questions. Can I thank members for their
patience and assistance in view of the difficulty we had with microphones today.
13 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7795
DEBATE ON PRIME MINISTER’S STATEMENT
Debate resumed from 12 February.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I am proud to be part of a
Government that is focused on the real issu es affecting New Zealanders and the real
progress that we are making as a country unde r Prime Minister John Key’s leadership. I
am sure every member in the House remembers that quote from President Bill Clinton:
“It’s the economy, stupid.”, and so it is for New Zealand in 2013. After reflecting on the
Prime Minister’s excellent speech, I was interested to see th e latest copy—the February
copy—of The Economist. I think we would all accept in th is House that it is one of the
world’s most respected magazines, in term s of challenging us in Government about
providing good governance. In that regular ma gazine is an articl e on the best-governed
countries in the world. It proceeds to list thos e countries that are t op of the class. I felt
incredibly proud to be part of a country that is list ed as the top of th e class in terms of
economic management. I want to point out that that report ranked New Zealand ahead
of Australia, ahead of the UK, ahead of Cana da, and ahead of the United States. For Mr
Peters’ benefit, New Zealand ranked ahead of Singapore.
In fact, it rates New Zealand as amongst the five top countries in terms of quality of
governance and in terms of supporting economic  growth. In terms of ease of doing
business, it ranked New Zealand third-best in the world. I say to the members in this
House that if we are genuinely concerned about jobs, and about giving New Zealand the
opportunities to go forward, we should be proud of  being a country that is the third-best
in the world to be able to set up new busine sses, because it is only those new businesses
that will enable us to create jobs. I think we would all welcome, as well, the latest
employment figures that show not only that New Zealand’s unemployment rate is better
than so many developed countries around the world that are struggl ing, but also that
those figures have come down. I also say th at we should welcome the whole range of
initiatives that the Prime Minister mentioned in his statement that are going to make a
contribution.
Let me just reflect on my own Nelson constituency and what it means in my own
area. Let us look at ultra-fast broadba nd—4,500 additional homes and businesses, as a
consequence of this Government’s programme, will have access to ultra-fast broadband.
Only last Saturday in my caravan at th e market, I met with a young business person, a
mechanical engineer, who currently does not have access to broadband and who is
looking forward to that roll- out to create jobs and opport unities in our area. I look
further at one of the biggest investments in science and research facilities in my home
community. The Cawthron Institute, an institute that we are very proud of, is embarking
this year on the bigg est investment in labs and expans ion in that organisation’s 90-year
history, and that is because of the sorts of partnerships the Cawthron Institute has with
this Government and its investment in research, which is part of that jobs machine.
I also want to note this month that the King Salmon aquaculture company is due to
get a decision on the final result for its new aquaculture farms in Marlborough Sounds.
Members opposite have vigorously opposed those new farms. They will provide an
extra 130 jobs in the top of the South Island. I say do not give me crocodile tears about
unemployment when you oppose initiatives like those from King Salmon that will
provide jobs for New Zealanders. I particul arly challenge the Green Party, which made
a submission to the board of inquiry opposing any expansion of aquaculture in my part
of the world. I say that that is one of the mo st job-rich opportunities that exist in the top
of the South Island.
7796 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 13 Feb 2013
I also want to actually congratulate my colleagues, both Hekia Parata and Paula
Bennett, for what they are doing in education and social welfare.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Members opposite may laugh, but let me tell them what it
means for real people—

items.speaker: Hon Clayton Cosgrove
items.text: Oh yeah? We’ll deliver some real people and they can tell
you.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: In February—this month, Mr Co sgrove—a teen parent unit
opened up in my electorate. What do memb ers opposite say about those teenage parents
who have for years been ignored by Minist ers of education and welfare? Members on
this side of the House know that teenage parents and their children are some of the most
at-risk groups of New Zealande rs, and I am proud to be part of a Government that is
actually investing in the facilities that will enable those teen age parents and their
children to be able to get an education.
On the subject of jobs, I read the sco ffing criticism from Labour members of the
Prime Minister’s initiative around the new cycleways. Let me say this to members
opposite—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Yeah, that’s right—how many jobs promised? How many delivered?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Phil Goff, let me tell you how many. I challenge Mr Goff to
do this: come on a bike ride—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Just answer the question.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Just take a breath— just take a breath, Mr Goff. I challenge
Phil Goff to come with me to Brightwater. Come with me to Brightwater, because right
opposite the post office that Phil Goff and hi s Government closed is a new restaurant
and caff. I went down the cycleway the w eekend before last to check out the new
cycleway. You know, I had to wait an hour an d a half for a coffee because there were
more than a hundred people who had done the cycleway. Let me give you another
example, Mr Goff, on the cycleway: a new business has opened up between my
electorate and Damien O’Connor’s. A new cycleway barge now operates between
Rabbit Island and M āpua. And do you know what my expe rience was again? I went to
catch the ferry—the new cycle ferry, the ne w little business that has started up as a
consequence of John Key’s initiative. It is a ferry that will take 50 bikes, and I could not
get on it because there were that many peopl e who were enjoying it. Damien O’Connor
is celebrating its success while his colleague Phil Goff criticises the cycleway initiative.
It is a positive initiative and every New Zealander knows it.
Then let us look at where the Opposition has gone in my area of new responsibility
in respect of housing. First of all, we got this dream from Mr Shearer last year that
Labour is going to build 100,000 homes at $300,000 each, and those members
specifically said, and put the little brochure out, that they were  three-bedroom houses.
How long did that policy commitment last? Ho w long did it last? It was not a matter of
a few days and Mr Shearer was backtracking on that promise. But I have to at least give
the Greens credit for saying how their unaffo rdable housing policies would actually be
funded. The Greens said that they are going to  rob the National Land Transport Fund to
put up the billions of dolla rs for the new houses. My question for Labour members:
100,000 houses, $300,000 each—and there is not a me mber of this House who truly
believes that can be delivered, but even s o—where is the $30 billion coming from? Can
you please tell us? Are you going to rake the debt up by another $30 billion? Are you
going to join the printing press, as the Greens have promised? There is absolutely no
credibility to that policy until Labour is pr epared to say where the 30 billion bucks is
coming from.
13 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7797
We on this side of the House are focuse d on housing affordability, but on the real
issues. There was a very substantive repo rt produced by the Pr oductivity Commission.
The Productivity Commission was actually an initiative created by this Government,
and the foundations for improving housing a ffordability lie in that report’s
recommendations around what we need to do with land supply and what we need to do
in terms of improving productivity with the sort of work that my colleague Steven Joyce
is doing in the area of skills training and apprenticeships. It is the sort of work that we
need to do in terms of improving competition and building materials, and the sort of
work we need to do like Maurice Williamson’s work in the compliance costs. If New
Zealanders are concerned about  housing affordability, the s ubstantive agenda that this
Government has set out gives New Zealanders the sort of hope and ambition that we all
want and stand for in this Government.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: The member Dr Nick Smith, who just
resumed his seat, said that New Zealande rs are concerned about housing affordability.
Of course they are, Dr Smith, because the statistics that came out 2 weeks ago showed
that New Zealand has become in the last fe w years one of the countries with the least
affordable housing for low-income people. This  Government is at the start of its fifth
year in office and this Minister of Housing says that he is now working on some plans
to deal with the housing crisis. The housing crisis has been there for 5 years. Young
people cannot get into their first home unless th ey have help from their parents. This
Government has sat on the sidelines, it has twiddled its thumbs, and it has done nothing
while house prices have soared, rents have  gone up, and we have a crisis of housing
shortage and affordability.
It is the fifth year of this party in Gove rnment, and I remember the first year, when
we had a job summit. The Job Summit turned out to be exactly what I said—a talkfest.
And there was the cycleway. John Key said th at that was going to produce thousands of
jobs. How many did it produce? A couple of  hundred—a couple of hundred. I want to
talk about the reality of jobs. I opened a new supermarket, Countdown in Stoddard
Road in Mount Roskill, on the day after Waitangi Day. Lovely new supermarket, great
manager—Mike Uri—

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Possible under the RMA changes.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: —and 120 jobs—120 jobs. I was real ly pleased to have 120 new
jobs in my electorate. But I said to Mike : “How many people, Mike, applied for those
jobs?”. Mr Joyce, do you know what the answer to that question was?

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: It was 2,600—2,600 people applied for 120 relatively low-paid
jobs in my electorate.
That is the reality of the legacy of stu ff-ups in providing jobs and skill training and
getting the economy going in th is country. I remember J ohn Key saying in 2009: “Next
year we’ll move aggressively towards dropping unemployment.” The latest figures, last
week, showed that in the last quarter of last year there was a net loss of 23,000 jobs. We
had the lowest level of labour force part icipation, Mr Joyce, in 10 years. This
Government has failed, and it has failed in every way. What  about the restructuring and
the mismanagement of that in the Ministry  of Foreign Affairs and Trade? Did this
Government accept responsibility? No. Murray McCully bravely blamed his head of
department. Then there was the Defence Fo rce. There was 22.6 percent attrition last
year, Mr Joyce, in the Navy in Auckland—22. 6 percent—and the lowest morale in the
Ongoing Attitude Survey since that survey began.
But I want to talk about another couple of botch-ups. There is  the education botch-
up. What did I hear John Key say? “Hek ia Parata is one of the smoothest
communicators in politics.” Well, Mr Speak er might have some  thoughts about that.
7798 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 13 Feb 2013
Five times today he asked her to answer th e question, and she ne ver did. If the Prime
Minister is going to be sacking incompeten t Ministers—that is why, apparently, he
sacked Phil Heatley and Kate Wilkinson, wit hout the respect of even letting them know
in advance, to show that he was the tough guy—why did he leave Hekia Parata and
Craig Foss in their positions?

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Why has your guy not done any reshuffles at all, eh?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Surely, they are the least comp etent Ministers, not only in the
House now but also as long as I can re member. Novopay—yeah, you are meant to be
the fix-up man, Mr Joyce, but why did the st uff-up happen in the first place? Why did
three Ministers sign off on that programme?  Why can she not answer the questions?
Why is she closing schools in Christchurch, adding to the trauma of people affected by
the earthquake? Why did she close the Salisbury School, when the court ruled her action
illegal? Why did she try to increase class si zes, when the Prime Minister said in the
Listener that he sent his kids to private school s because they had lo wer class sizes and
then said to everybody else: “Oh, it won’t affect you.”? A to tal botch-up. A total botch-
up in education. It is not good e nough. It is not fair on our ki ds and the future we want
to provide for them.
But I want to touch on another botch-up now, and this was first raised in the House
by my colleagues Clayton Cosgrove and Da mien O’Connor. It was the botch-up over
the handling of the issue of contamination of  our dairy products by dicyandiamide. Let
us get one thing right at the start: dicyandiamide is not a health or food safety issue. It is
not a health or food safety issue, but, Mr Joyce, it is a contamination issue, and it is an
issue about reputation and about  branding. We go out into the world, as I did for years
as Minister of Trade, proudly promoting this country as “100% Pure New Zealand”, and
this issue comes along. For 4 long months af ter Fonterra realis ed it was a problem,
nothing happened. Nothing was said by this Government until the contamination was
released to the public by a media article in the Wall Street Journal. I feel sorry for our
ambassador in Beijing, Carl Worker—a comp etent diplomat. And what did Mr Worker
have to say? He was clearly left out of th e loop. Four months after this Government
knew about the problem, he was forced to go out and say that it wa s “regrettable” that
New Zealand did not forewarn Chinese author ities, which led to, he said, “confusion
and unnecessary doubt”.
I remember when we had the melamine crisis and the San Lu company, and I tell
you, our Cabinet came together within 24 hours in an emergency meeting and had
informed the Chinese authoritie s within that time frame. We  headed off a disaster, we
headed off a crisis, because it was “New Zealand Inc.” It was Ministers working
together, talking to each other. I want to know when the Minister for Primary Industries
told the Minister of Trade and the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and then I want to know
why none of them said anything publicly until they were forced to because it was
revealed publicly. In fact, Clayton Cosgrove was respondi ng to things the Minister
should have been responding to, 5 days be fore the Minister would even make a
comment. I say this: why did the Chinese Government a nd the Chinese public learn
about the problem only through an article in the Wall Street Journal  that described the
contamination as “toxic”? It was not toxic, bu t the perception was left that it must have
been because New Zealand had tried to cover it over.
Why were we not open and transparent? Why were we not proactive about this
problem so we could head it off and stop a ny damage? China is our biggest market. I
fought hard to get a free-trade  agreement with it. We have trebled our exports to that
country, and I do not want to see this proud legacy of a Labour Government trampled
upon by an incompetent National Government that cannot handle these issues right.
China Central Television has an audience of millions—hundreds of millions. They were
13 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7799
running this and headlining this as a scandal. A weibo, which is China’s Twitter, ran
thousands of postings from pe ople expressing con cern. It ran a survey  where over half
of the respondents said that they did not trust and they were not sure about the quality or
safety of New Zealand dairy products. That should never have happened. It did not need
to happen, and a competent Government would have prevented it from happening.
Let us look at what Biopure Health said. It is one of the Kiwi exporters. It said that it
was a public relations disaster for this Gove rnment—a public relations disaster. That is
a front-line company. It said that its pr oducts, which had been doubling in value and
sales every week, went to zero—went to ze ro. There is another company, New Image,
which is a baby formula exporter.  It said that the industry was in damage control, and it
blamed the Government for the lack of warn ing. I want to say th is: I hope that this
problem can now be contained. It is in all of our interests as New Zealanders that it is.
But, surely, the Prime Minister, John Key, and this incompetent National Government
need to learn the lessons from it. Be proactiv e, have a strategy, be open and transparent,
head it off, and protect New Zealand’s inte rests—those are the responsibilities of a
Government, and this National Government failed in those responsibilities.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think, once
again, we are seeing a demonstration that there is nothing that Labour will not stoop to
to talk down the New Zealand economy for its ow n political gains. Actually, it is sort of
ironic that the member Phil Goff referred to his role in the China free-trade agreement
in which, of course, he had a role, and yet he  sits on the same side of the House as a
member who late last year was criticisi ng the Chinese company Haier for purchasing
Fisher and Paykel Appliances and saying that  that was not necessarily a good thing for
New Zealand. So this Opposition needs to sort ou t its lines in terms of the role of trade
in New Zealand’s future, the role of our rela tionships with our trading partners, and our
role with our second-largest trading partne r. But, of course, co nsistency is not the
Opposition’s strong point.
The other thing we heard in that speech was an approach that, once again, seeks to
ignore the world in consider ing New Zealand’s economic progress. I am proud to be
part of a Government that has worked so hard over the last 4 years to give this country a
much better outcome from the global financial crisis than most other countries in the
OECD, as well as dealing with the second shock—which the other countries did not
have to deal with—which was the Canterbu ry earthquakes in our second-largest city.
The other side keeps trying to pretend that those twin shocks to New Zealand did not
occur, and of course they did.
So we come to the start of 2013 and the st ate of play for New Zealand in the Prime
Minister’s address at the start of Parliament . There is a huge range of things that this
Government is working on to encourage the growth of the New Zealand economy, and
we are seeing some very good progress for Ne w Zealand. The cost of living in New
Zealand is low, savings rates are up, a nd, yes, we are making good economic progress.
And as was pointed out by my co lleague the Hon Dr Nick Smith, The Economist has
highlighted the well way in which this country is being economically managed.
There is a very clear contrast between both sides of the House. On this side of the
House we understand that for more jobs and more growth you have to have more
investment from the private sector. So we are out there, working constantly to create
those opportunities for New Zeal anders by trying to remove the impact of things that
get in the way of that investment, and looki ng at things like our e xport markets. Again,
it is ironic that Phil Goff was up, talking about  trade, when Labour’s coalition partners
the Greens are opposed to probably the biggest trade agreement that New Zealand could
see in the next 10 years—the trans-Pacific trade partnership.
7800 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 13 Feb 2013
We also have Labour’s other putative co alition partner not doing us proud on the
international stage in terms of our relati onships with our trad ing partners, but doing
things like criticising high-value Chinese t ourists coming to this country and having the
opportunity to tour here, like other countries , and saying that that is something that
should not occur.
So what you have is all these Oppositio n parties that talk a good game around
growth, but, fundamentally, they are opposed to  pretty much most things that would
deliver that growth in New Zealand. I have  made a helpful list. Of course, Opposition
parties opposed the law changes for The Hobbit —and they still oppose them even
today. I am thrilled that they spend their time opposing those law changes, because they
keep reminding New Zealanders that they opposed a law change to help an industry
grow in this country.
And then they opposed the Resource Management Act changes—the ones that we
have had and the ones that  we are proposing. They do no t even know what we are
proposing yet, but we can guarantee that th ey are opposed to it. They are opposed to
plans to build the Auckland convention centre. They have put every single roadblock in
the way of that that they possibly could. Th ey are opposed to oil and gas exploration on
the East Coast. Their energy and resources spokesperson said that  gas was not going
anywhere, so we should just leave it there. Well, tell that to the people of the East Coast
who would like the jobs. And, of  course, they have been op posed, and, at best in the
case of Labour, lukewarm, to hydraulic fracturing.
I mentioned they are opposed to the inve stment of Haier in Fisher and Paykel
Appliances. They are opposed to speeding up Bathurst Resources Ltd’s resource
consents at Denniston. They are opposed to Chinese investment in New Zealand
generally, particularly if they have had a focus group recently. They are opposed to tax
changes to encourage productive investme nt. They are opposed to irrigation. The
Greens are absolutely opposed to irrigation;  Labour is sort of having a bob each way.
They are opposed to lessening the emissions  trading scheme costs on trade-exposed
business.
All those things encourage investment in j obs and growth in this country. So as the
Prime Minister said at the start of this y ear, this Government is focused on making New
Zealand a magnet for investment for jobs and growth. And what are the Labour Party
and the Green Party doing? They are busy tr ying out some new slogans. They have a
couple of new slogans that they are running at the moment. The interesting one for them
is one they have obviously been looking at online in a few of the speeches from the UK.
This one is so-called hands-on Government. Th at is the sort of thing they are focus-
grouping at the moment—hands-on Government . Well, let me tell you this. Hands-on
Government, the slogan of the Labour Party, means only one thing—hands on your
pockets. It means hands on your money. That is  what hands-on means. They are against
every form of private sector investment. Th ey want to reach furt her into the nation’s
pockets, and spend more money, because th ey know how to do it better. That is
Labour’s approach to growth, and what th at means is growth in New Zealand’s
overdraft and growth in New Zealand’s deficit.
Labour members have a progra mme called “Kiwi Broke”. It is a building scheme. It
is a code for big-borrowing and big-spendi ng Government. So they have made up a
rinky-dinky, taxpayer-funded scheme, which, ju st like all their other taxpayer-funded
schemes, will cost only a little bit—only a little bit. It will actually cost five to 10 times
what they say and deliver one-tenth of the re sults. We had that. We threw that out in
2008 because these people know only how to stick their hands in your pockets. That is
what they mean by hands-on Government—hands on your wallet.
13 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7801
That is the Labour Party’s approach in 2013—or , at least, we think it is, because the
only thing we have heard from it this year was its pro tem leader backtracking on its
policy. He got up and did his state of the nati on speech at the start of  the year and said:
“Oh, by the way, it will probably cost 550, maybe 450 grand a house,  not really 300.
Maybe 550.”, and you are sitting there thinking: “That’s all he ’s got to offer—that he
has to back down on a policy he announced pr ior to Christmas.” And, of course, not
surprisingly, he has got a little maths probl em of his own now, because he started the
year, apparently—there are rumours—with 10 abstentions in his caucus vote, it was
reported.

items.speaker: Todd McClay
items.text: Who were they?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: We do not know who they are yet, although we could
probably do a quick sweepstake. So th e guy was the only one standing for the
leadership of the Labour Party, and he got nailed by 10 of his own side who refused to
vote for him. That is what happened at the cau cus vote, and the reason is that he has not
said a thing this year except that the “Kiwi Broke” policy is already broke, and that is
his problem.
So on one side of the House you have a crow d that believes the solution is to dig
further and deeper into people’s pockets, recycle the money, and look like they are
doing something. On the other side of the House there is a Government that is
absolutely focused on encouraging investment in productive industries in this country—
and we are not confusing that with job subs idies, which is the Gr eens’ approach. Their
definition of investment is that if the G overnment does it, it must be good. I am telling
the Greens that the reality is that if  you look around and you are doing something, and
there is nobody else there, it is not an investment; it a job subsidy scheme. The Greens
sit very nicely with the Labour Party, because th at is what it wants to do. It wants to get
its hands in your pocket. We are very focused on making New Zealand a more attractive
place for investment, for higher-paying jobs, and for higher growth in 2013. Thank you.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak in this debate on
the Prime Minister’s statement and to follo w the Minister for Economic Development,
Steven Joyce. What a wonderful outlook the Minister has shown Ne w Zealanders is in
store for them over this coming year. Before I get into some of the detail of what a hard-
working Government we are, I say to Minister  Joyce that we almost do not have to say
that any more. After 4 years and another elec tion, New Zealanders have recognised that
they have a hard-working Government. They to ld all of us a year ago they wanted a
hard-working Government—[Interruption]—and guess what, members opposite? They
voted for a hard-working Government.
Mr Speaker, I want to wish you the very best, as this is the first time I have spoken in
the House this year, and say I look forward to working with you. But I also want to pay
a particular compliment to the former Sp eaker Dr The Rt Hon Lockwood Smith, and to
thank him for his many, many years of servi ce to this House and to New Zealand and
New Zealanders. I look forward very much to hearing from him later on this afternoon.
What a sad occasion it will be for members opposite that Dr Smith is making his last
speech and leaving the House. No longer will th ey feel that they should take points of
order in question time asking him to protect them. I am grateful that he offered them
little protection in his time as Speaker.
What I want to do is touch on two things th at I think are very important. The first is
an excellent announcement today by the Mini ster of Police, the Hon Anne Tolley,
around supporting police more a nd giving our police force th e tools to get on and do
what New Zealanders want them to do, and that is to police. That is a fantastic
announcement. But, firstly, to set the scene, what has happened over the last 4 years that
we have been the Government? Before we took office, I remember standing on the
7802 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 13 Feb 2013
campaign trail in the Rotorua electorate. At  the time that seat was held by a former
Labour member of Parliament who is no long er in this Parliament. We were talking
about crime, and every statistic that came out showed New Zealanders that the last
Labour Government lost track of what it shoul d be doing and that crime statistics were
getting worse. We heard all the reasons fo r this: it was difficult, and, you know, it was
the police’s fault, and everything else.
What I can say is that this  Government has backed the police force and given it the
tools. In the fiscal year of 2010, we sa w a 7 percent decrease  in reported crime
throughout New Zealand—7 percent decrease  throughout the whole of New Zealand.
After everything Labour said to us previous ly when in Government—that it was on top
of it and it had a lot to do with the moon and the stars and the weather and so on. But
was that a one-off? In the 2011-12 fiscal ye ar there was a 5.9 percent drop in reported
crime throughout New Zealand. Is that importa nt? Well, this is a bout New Zealanders
being safer in their homes and in their streets. It is about the police being able to get out
and do what it is we want them to do, to police effectively, givi ng them the tools and
making sure they know the Government fully supports them in their job, and for them to
be arresting those who choose to break th e law and holding them to account on behalf
of all law-abiding New Zealanders.
This reduction in crime is a wonderful thi ng. I want to look at my electorate for a
moment. In 2011 there was a 3.4 pe rcent decrease in crime. You have to go back a long
way, before we came to Government, to find any other decrease in crime in the Rotorua
electorate. In 2010 there was a 5 percent decrease in crime.  That is about 9 percent
accumulatively over those 2 years. And, impr essively, there have been drops in
burglaries, illicit drugs, weapon offences, robberies, and extortion. Robberies and
extortion are down by about 11.5 percent in th at period of time. Burglary is down 10.7
percent, and drug offences are down 8.4 percen t. That means that all over New Zealand
thousands of law-abiding citizens have not become victims of crime, because of the
work the police are doing. That  is thousands of people in New Zealand who are able to
get on with their jobs and not worry about wh at those who decide to commit crimes are
doing in their homes or in their streets. This  has happened in part because of the great
support that the Government and our Minister have given the police, but also because of
the wonderful job our policemen and poli cewomen do every single day on our behalf.
They do a fantastic job under extremely difficult circumstances.
Last year the Bay of Plen ty police force’s combined drug campaign resulted in 178
arrests, 27,000 cannabis plants destroyed, and many methamphetamine dealers and
traders arrested. Police conf iscated—this is frightening—26 firearms that were held
illegally and could have been used to comm it offences. That means that in the Bay of
Plenty we are safer becaus e of the job this Governme nt has done—it has given the
police the tools they need—and because of th e hard work the police do on our behalf
every day. I know that my constituents realise this and like this and support our police
force, and they want us as a Government to hold criminal s to account. In October last
year I was given the honour to come and speak at the inaugural meeting of the Sensible
Sentencing Trust’s branch in Rotorua. It was a large room, and it was full to
overflowing with people who have had enough;  who said that they support what the
Government is doing, they support our police force, and they believe that those who
commit crimes must be held to account. Peter Bentley, who heads that up in Rotorua, is
doing quite an amazing job.
So the announcement today—what is this about? See, the Government has got a plan
to allow the police and to allow other civil servants to get on and do the job that we
want them to do, not to bind them or hold them back with unnecessary red tape and
bureaucracy. What I want to say is that the work that the Minister Anne Tolley has done
13 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7803
over the last year since she became Minist er of Police is fantastic and is paying
dividends today. One of our prio rities this term is to deliver Better Public Services, and
her announcement today was that there will be 6,500 front-line police officers—and you
have got to remember that over the la st 3 years we have delivered 1,000 more
policemen to the front line, which was an election pledge on our behalf and different
from what the last Government said it woul d do. It said it would have more policemen
and actually could not deliver on that. Well, we did. We delivered more policemen and
policewomen on the front line.
For 6,500 of them, the announcement today sa id that they will receive smartphones
by mid-2014, and 3,900 staff will receive tablets. And the reason this is important is that
it will free up half a million hours of police time for them to do their job on the front
line—half a million hours of extra time when our police can be out in our communities,
in our streets, finding those who commit crimes against so me of the most vulnerable
people in our society and holding them to account. This is wonderful. In the Bay of
Plenty, that is 41,526 hours that will be sa ved in that district each year—41,000. So
what you will hear at the next election is a Labour Opposition complaining, whining,
and running up and down the country trying  to scare hard-wor king, law-abiding New
Zealanders that this Government has not go t a commitment to the police force. But not
only did we increase the number of policemen on the front line; we have been able to
free up half a million hours for them to do their jobs.
Do you remember those stories in the news paper where mums and dads were saying
they called a policeman but could not get th rough to him because he was stuck in the
back office doing paperwork? Well, this is ha lf a million hours out on our streets in my
electorate and other electorates. In the Bay of Plenty, we ar e giving our policemen
41,000 extra hours. Is that important? Well, wh en I get the chance to go and talk to
them and thank them for the job that th ey are doing on our behalf in Kawerau, in
Rotorua, in Murupara, and in ot her parts of my electorate, th ey tell me that what they
enjoy doing most is being out in the co mmunity, making sure people are safe, and
arresting criminals. This Government has give n them yet another tool to get out and to
do that.
I want to say again to the Minister and our Prime Minister, thank you on behalf of
our police force for deciding that we will support it come thick or thin. Is that not such a
change from what happened over 9 years of a Labour Government, when the police felt
unwanted and unused, and were pu t in a back office to do th eir work? Law and order is
a great priority for this Government. It is somethi ng that you will hear much more
about, but I give you a pledge on behalf of my self as a local MP and on behalf of the
Government that we will continue to do ev erything possible to make New Zealanders
safer and we will do everything possible to support our police force.
I look forward next week to the Law and Order Committee coming forward and
perhaps sending back to this House a very im portant piece of legisl ation, another great
tool for our police and another great way for us to make New Zealanders safer. I see
members opposite nodding. They want to suppor t this very important bill to ban the
wearing of gang insignia in all Governme nt buildings throughout  New Zealand. This
will get on top of gangs, which do nothi ng but intimidate, commit crime, harm
vulnerable New Zealanders, and sell drugs to our children. In  the words of a member of
the New Zealand First Party, we do not fear them. We want to give the police tools to
make sure that they know what they are doing and they can get amongst them, disrupt
them, arrest them, and, where absolutely necessary, send them to jail.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. T ēnā
koutou huri noa, ngā mema o te Whare.
7804 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 13 Feb 2013
[Greetings to you, Mr Speaker, and to you, collectively, members throughout the
House.]
I am very pleased to make the final contribution from the Labour Party in opposition
to the Prime Minister’s stat ement. It has been just over 2 weeks since the Prime
Minister stood before this House and the na tion and so sneeringly told us what a great
start to the year it has b een. He delivered the speech in  that John Key jokey manner,
which really just screams insincerity. For 4 years we have had carefully crafted excuses
as to why this country of ours is getting now here and why we cannot get ahead. It is the
fault of the global financial crisis, it is the fault of the Canterbury earthquakes, or it is
the fault of the illuminati, or some other fanc iful excuse. It is the fault of everyone but
the National Government.
Could it be that this countr y is getting nowhere because we have a Government that
refuses to take direction and show some lead ership? It is hands-off.  It is rich of Mr
Joyce to talk about focus groups when we know that he had a whole book written about
him as one of The Hollow Men , in terms of focus groups, Crosby/Textor, and strategic
communication consultants—all of those sort s of carryings-on that we know underpin
this very poor National Government.
I want to focus on three things that are d ear to me: kids, poverty, and health. Last
year there came out damning statistics on child poverty. They were really sorry reading.
The statistics showed that too many kids live in unhealthy homes.  They are going to
school tired and hungry and have zero chance of learning under that sort of regime.
Although we all know it is wrong to identi fy schools by their decile rating, the fact
of the matter is th at it is the decile 1, 2, and 3 school s that have the br eakfast clubs, not
the decile 10 schools. You see, in the Prime Minister’s perfect world everyone is as rich
as he is, or they should pull themselves up by their bootstraps and reach for the stars. It
is the same with this Nati onal caucus. But they  would not know Struggle Street. They
do not know about Struggle Street.

items.speaker: Here is a scary thought
items.text: if you are Māori or Polynesian and living in this country you
definitely are on a road to nowhere, or you are flocking to the departure lounge and
heading, like 350,000 other Kiwis,  over to Australia. But do  not blame Labour for it,
blame the National Government. It is the one  with the Ministers who fail to understand
the clients it serves. We al ready know the two casualties. Kate Wilkinson is gone. Phil
Heatley was no good as a housing Minister and he is gone, although he did mention in a
select committee today that he is down but not out, and good luck to him.
Now when we look at the state of the hous ing market, we see it has blown out. We
know that there is another property bubble th at is getting bigger and bigger in this
country. The Government has made it too e xpensive to build the Kiwi dream, because
the parameters on the Reserve Bank are too narrow. Inflation targeting is not working in
the context that we are in now. The worl d is awash with debt. Countries around the
world are debasing their currencies, and it is just putting more pressure on our currency
and crippling our manufacturing sector a nd our export base. So there are many, many
things that are suffering right across our economy.
I turn to Christchurch. There is not enough housing stock in Christchurch. There is a
crisis down there. The ones that have been shafted by the Government and the greedy
landlords of Christchurch are the same old M āori and Polynesian wh ānau, who have
limited resources and even less money and/or jobs. Rents have gone up  in that city and
it has forced wh ānau into seriously overcrowded si tuations, which has led to poor
health.
Children from these environments are going to school every day tired, sick, and
hungry, and so are unable to learn anything—that is if they are goi ng to school at all.
Nowadays we have the real problem of ki ds not going to school, because they cannot
13 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7805
afford basic tools for learni ng—basic things like statione ry. Kids are not going to
school, because mum and dad cannot afford just basic things.
That is the type of New Zealand that th is Government has created. It is a New
Zealand where kids live in substandard housing and poverty, where kids go to school, if
they are lucky, on a packet of 2-minute noodles—a nd that is if they ha ve eaten at all. It
has created an environment wh ere if your child gets a stre p throat it leads to some
serious diseases. It is tough being a little kid in this c ountry, especially so when you are
broke. But New Zealand is not a poor country . We are a rich country, but we have a
problem with how wealth is spread.
This Government is too concerned with accumulating wealth at the top end of society
while leaving just little crumbs for everyone below. It is a “me” approach to governing,
a winner-takes-all approach to society, a nd it is wrong. That is why the Anglican
Church’s Family Centre has ca lculated that we need a liv ing wage, and that $18 to $20
an hour is what is necessary to provide workers and their families with the basic
necessities of life. Under this Government, 750,000 people earn less than, or about, that
amount—that is, the number of working poor  in this country has ballooned. Even
beginner teachers, who most would say are skil led workers, earn less than that amount.
Not only is this a Government of low expectation but it is a Government of low wages.
I want to turn now to training and education, because we have spoken a lot about and
heard a lot about that in this debate. You know, 90,000 rangatahi ac ross the country are
not in employment, education, or training. T hose are horrific numbers. We have figures
that show that the unemployment rate for M āori and Pacific is three times higher than it
is for Pākehā. What do we hear out of the Prime Mi nister? As we heard in his statement
to the House, this is the Gove rnment that actually trains people as opposed to spending
money and getting absolutely no result—and th is is the rub; it is wasting millions of
dollars of taxpayers’ money. One word: Novopay.
If anyone needs a better example of a Government wasting millions of taxpayer
dollars and getting no results it is “no-pay Novopay”. We have heard that it is costing
the Government over $5 million, and then it  has got commissions of inquiry as well,
trying to rectify the mess. It  is an absolute mess. “Novopay” has become the new word
in the Kiwi lexicon for a tota l and complete balls-up. Minister  Parata is right at the top
of it. She signed it off. And she is defin itely not the smooth communicator, because she
is umming and ahing—she really is in the hot seat—and getting grilled by my colleague
there, Mr Hipkins, and long may it continue.
Last week we had the terrible news about  the Mainzeal Property and Construction
receivership. If the Government is talking up how great our economy is, I say that
Mainzeal’s demise is a huge blow to the whole construction industry and also to the
many hundreds of thousands of workers and su bcontractors who were  all supported by
that enterprise. The Government is screaming for apprenticeships and skilled workers—
or so we think—for Christch urch. When young men who want to be trained as brickies
or chippies go to a Mainzeal si te, see that that site is cl osed down, and see contractors
who are not even able to go in there a nd get their tools, those young men will think
twice about taking up a career in the constr uction industry. So we are not actually
attracting new apprenticeships.
What does the Government want to do? It wants to fly in cheap labour from
overseas. But the biggest scandal of all fo r this Government is the record high
unemployment, 7.3 percent. As I said before, the unemployment rate for M āori and
Pacific is three times that for P ākehā. That is the highest rate since the last National
Government in the 1990s. Again it blames the global financial crisis, soft demand
overseas, and the Labour Government. But the Labour Government left the lowest
7806 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 13 Feb 2013
unemployment rate in the OECD and low publ ic debt. The blame lies squarely at the
feet of this National Government.
I am proud of the new initi atives that Labour has a nnounced. With our KiwiBuild
policy we will get more low to middle inco me earners into affordable housing and
increase the supply. If anyone talks about  numbers, about what $300,000 will get you, I
just say haere mai ki Te Wai Pounamu, come  to the South Island. In Blenheim you will
get a three-bedroom home for $249,000, four bedrooms in Dunedin for $270,000, and in
Lumsden you can get a three or four-b edroom home for $69,000 to $159,000. If you
want to be real landed gentry you can go to  Lumsden and get 4.6 hectares of land for—
wait for it—$165,000, and the $135,000 that you have left over will probably get you a
home and a rental property. There are ma ny opportunities for affordable housing, and
we are looking right across the country, and not  with an Auckland-centric view of the
world. I am very proud that across the M āori electorate there are many opportunities for
that housing development, that KiwiBuild policy to take place.
We do oppose this Government. We oppose everyt hing that it is about. It is right; we
are left. It is blue; we are red. It is ugly, and we are the attractive opposite. We are ready
to take this Government down come 2014, becau se the people out th ere definitely want
a change. Kia ora anō tātou.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Obviously, it has been an inte resting afternoon in the House
with some challenges with our sound syst em. I know our technicians are working
incredibly hard to sort the situation out for us.
I do want to just say before I start my contribution in the debate on the Prime
Minister’s statement that I want to wish the Dr The Rt Hon Lockwood Smith farewell
this afternoon and th ank him for his service in the H ouse and for his 4 years as the
Speaker, and to wish the incoming Speaker, th e Rt Hon David Carter , all the best. He
did an incredible job today, despite the sound system being off, so I think we have got
some great things ahead of us.
Speaking of great things ahead  of us, I am really proud to  be a Kiwi, and I think we
have got great opportunities in front of us . I think the last contribution from Rino
Tirikatene, a Labour speaker opp osite, says it all. It wa s there in black and white,
categoric—those members will oppose anything that National puts up. Well, actually, I
think that is kind of stupid, a nd lots of New Zealanders out there also agree, because at
the end of the day if it is a good idea, and if it is going to solve some of the challenges
that ordinary hard-working New Zealanders are facing, then I actually think the Labour
Party should look at it.  It should start thinki ng about using the word  “yes” from time to
13 Feb 2013 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 7807
time, instead of just, black and white, saying no to everything this side of the House
suggests. At the end of the da y it is saying no to economic growth, it is saying no to
jobs, and it is saying no to food on the tables of the kids that it pur ports to protect on a
daily basis. That is why I think that it is just absolutely ridiculous for a member opposite
to make that kind of statement in this House.
If we come to this Parliament representing a constituency with the intention of
making a better New Zealand, we might have different pathways, but each and every
one of us should hold dear to that commitment that we serve in this place to make New
Zealand a better country. That is definitely  why I came to this place, and why I am
proud to be a member of the National Party Government led so ably by Prime Minister
John Key. This is about making sure that th e opportunities that New Zealand has—each
and every one of us being able to make th e most of them. Yes, we have faced some
challenges as a country. I think the member who just resumed his seat must have had his
head buried in the sand not to take into consideration a ny of the sorts of challenges this
Government has faced, both financial and natura l disasters, that have led to some of the
most difficult and challenging economic circum stances ever faced. I would invite that
member to get his head out of the sand and actually start looking at the circumstances
this country has faced over th e 4 years and the work that th is Government is doing, and
continues to do, with a robust economic plan that has been detailed in, now, five out of
six documents in terms of our Business Growth Agenda.
I sat next to a gentleman on a plane just last week and we had a conversation about
debt. The conversation was around why is it that the Prime Minister’s opening
conversation in any speech is about the economy. The reality is that it has to be—it has
to be right now. He asked me why is it that  we are so determined to get our books back
and balanced. I thought, well, it is no different—it is no different—to what you do at
home. It is no different to wh at businesses do. It is no differe nt for us as a Government
to have to make sure that we get on top of our debt and we start paying it down. This
side of the House actually has a very robust plan for making that happen. That side of
the House, unfortunately, just wants to go out and print more money and rack up more
debt for generations to come. So it was an  interesting conversat ion I had with this
gentleman on the plane in terms of, very pl ainly and very simply, why the economy is
the No. 1 priority for this Government.
It was really interesting being at the Busi ness New Zealand Back  to the Grindstone
meeting last night. You could have heard a pin drop. Despite th ere being hundreds of
people in the town hall—it was really in teresting—you could not hear a pin drop when
the Prime Minister spoke, because the people  in that room—and they were not just
business people; they were scientists, they we re trade unionists, they were all sorts of
people from all sorts of organisations—wer e listening very carefully to the Prime
Minister, because they know that this Government has a plan, which we are following.
It was really interesting to see how on boa rd that whole room was in following the
direction, under challenging circumstances and difficult times, that the Prime Minister is
leading.
One of the things that I did want to just speak about is the issue of investment. Again,
it came up in the conversation last night at the Business New Zealand event. In terms of
creating jobs, it is busine sses—businesses employ people.  It is not up to the
Government to create jobs. The Government ’s job is to create the environment that
allows businesses the confiden ce to grow and to take on new staff. One of the things
that really holds businesses b ack, and one of the things I ha ve been talking to many of
the businesses in the Taup ō electorate about, is the challe nge of getting capital. That is
why this Government has put a significant pr iority on making it easier for businesses to
get capital.
7808 Debate on Prime Minister’s Statement 13 Feb 2013
One of the things that, again, that side of the House is very loud and proud about
saying no to is foreign investment. There are some significant projects in the Taup ō
electorate that would not happen if there was not foreign investment. There are jobs that
have been created in the Taupō electorate that would not have happened if it was not for
foreign investment. [Interruption] Members opposite do not seem  to listen. The foreign
investment in businesses in Taup ō has created jobs. So that is why it is really important
that we provide the right environment for foreign investment to come into this country
and that we make it easier for those invest ors to choose New Zealand as a place where
they would want to invest. The reality is that they have got lots of other places they can
choose—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: And they are.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: —and we want to encourage them to choose New Zealand.
Well, if the naysayers on that side say no more  often than not, then definitely they will
stay away. This Government is a Government that is interested in supporting businesses
to create jobs.
The other thing I want to speak about is th e power of our people. The thing that is
always really important to me, and that is incredibly important to this side of the House,
is boosting skills, and it starts in earl y childhood education. We  heard it today in
question time. Where is the focus for lifting achievement? The focus on lifting
achievement, first and foremost, is making sure that we have a larger  percentage of our
young children attending early childhood educa tion—98 percent is the target. One of
the things that I have been doing as a local MP is having c onversations with my
community and saying: “Well, how do we make sure that we achieve that 98 percent in
the Taupō electorate? Whether it is in Tūrangi, whether it is in Tokoroa, or whether it is
in Mangakin ō, how do we make that happen?”, b ecause it is important. Everywhere I
go, people know the importance of education, so we have got to focus on the barriers.
It was quite interesting to sit in a select committee and be part of hearing submissions
about concerns that submitters have about partnership schools. One of the submitters
talked about the fact that choice in education has caused inequality. So my question
was, then: “Well, which schools would you cl ose? If you don’t think that choice in
education and schools is good for student achievement, which ones would you suggest
you close?”. Of course, there was no answer to that, because at the end of the day
education is the thing that is important. Actually, this side of the House is quite
comfortable with the fact that parents should be able to make choices about where their
children go to school and, if their children are not achieving , to be able to support them
more with better information and better data . We want to invest in teachers and
principals to ensure that the quality of teaching is also increasing, because I, for one, am
very clear that education is the one thing th at creates equality of opportunity, and that is
why it is so critical for this side of the House.
We are setting targets for National Certificate of Educational Achievement level 2.
There were a few people who said, when we  started setting targets, that that was
challenging. Well, we are putting our mone y where our mouth is. We are actually
setting targets and focusing the Public Service on achieving what is important for New
Zealanders.
It has been my privilege to  speak in this debate. The Government has a very robust
and very detailed plan about how we ar e addressing the challenges in the economy,
about which members on that side of the H ouse want to keep their heads in the sand.
We have fantastic opportunitie s as a country. It is rea lly the opportunity for New
Zealanders to seize those opportunities and make the most of them. The Government on
this side of the House is supporting them , each and every step of the way, under the
very strong and decisive leadership of Prime Minister John Key.

So I want to speak about two areas that I have involvement in. One of those is in the

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: I am pleased to be supporti ng this Environment Canterbury
(Temporary Commissioners and Improved Water Management) Amendment Bill at its
second reading. Back in May 2010 the Environment Canterbury (Temporary
Commissioners and Improved Water Management) Act was passed. The bill that we are
looking at today will extend the governance arrangements under that Act and retain
Government-appointed commissioners instead  of elected members in the Canterbury
Regional Council until the election of 2016. There are also special  provisions in the bill
that will require a ministerial review in  2014 of Environment Canterbury’s governance
structure, its membership, its powers, and its functions.
At a previous debate on this bill the Hon Annette King had been talking loud and
long about how bad this bill will be for Ca ntabrians, but as so meone who lives in
Canterbury I know that she is wrong. The majority  of Cantabrians see this as a sensible
way forward during a very difficult time in our  province. To understand why they feel
like this, let us look at the history. Let us look at the history.
In 2010, following an extended  period of poor perfor mance, the Government
replaced Environment Canterbury councillo rs with commissioners. How did central
government know that Environment Canterbur y was performing badly? Firstly, it came
from other elected representatives in the province. They told us. The mayors across
Canterbury came to central government and as ked for intervention so that they could
better manage the regional council issues. So  we set up an independe nt review, and that
independent review found that Environment Canterbury granted consents without any
proper framework, and that it allowed new water to be taken for catchments that were
overallocated.
At the same time the 2007-08 Resource Management Act survey came out, and that
stated that Environment Canter bury had failed to process more than two-thirds of the
13 Feb 2013 Env. Canterbury (Temp. Commissioners etc.) Amdt Bill 7813
resource consent applications within the statutory time frame, and that actually
Environment Canterbury’s performance wa s the worst out of 84 councils in New
Zealand. The review group also stated that the institutional failure in Environment
Canterbury “requires comprehensive and ra pid intervention on the part of central
government to … enhance both regional and national well-being.”
So seven commissioners were appointed, with  Dame Margaret Bazley as the chair,
and I have to say they have been highly su ccessful and very effective in addressing
Environment Canterbury’s systemic problems  and reforming the quality of decision
making and conduct. More important, their wo rk has been totally transparent, with
public reporting to the people of Canterbury every 3 mont hs. During their time they
have managed the Canterbury Natural Resour ces Regional Plan through to an operative
stage and they have started working on a second-generation land and water plan—things
that had been hanging around Environment Canterbury for a very long time.
They have also made significant progress on the implementation of the Canterbury
Water Management Strategy. That was a stra tegy that came out of discussions across
the province. It is a very democratic way, a nd it is a really very collaborative process.
Through that process they have develope d zone implementation plans and are now
working their way into a statutory plan by wa y of planned change processes. The latest
survey results on the Resource Management Act show that they have dramatically
improved compliance with statutory consent time lines under the Resource Management
Act. Ninety-two percent of resource consents  were processed with in the statutory time
frames in 2010-11, compared with 29 percent in 2007-08.
They have also significantly improved relati onships with territorial authorities, with
iwi, and with other stakeholders, and thr ough collaboration they have come up with a
joint working programme with Ng āi Tahu. Finally, and very im portant in our province,
they have established a strong partnership with the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
Authority to facilitate earthquake recovery. So all in all it has been a very successful
body, and has delivered good results for the environment and for Canterbury.
It is really appropriate that central govern ment assists councils when a failure has
happened. Not acting can bring serious conseq uences for the future of Canterbury. The
commissioners have done an excellent job, and the people of Canterbury are happy to
see them continue their work until 2016. And how do I know that  the majority of
Cantabrians are supportive? Because  of their reactions to the bill. Let me read some of
their comments. Local Government New Z ealand, which represents the mayors, the
councillors, and the ratepayers, says: “T he Commission has made good headway on
major issues affecting the region … Envi ronment Canterbury has done outstanding
work, both in its response to the eart hquakes in Canterbury, and its work on
implementing the Canterbury Water Management Strategy,”.
And the rural community, Federated Farm ers and Irrigation New Zealand, has said:
“I would hope”—and I suggest that the Hon Clayton Cosgrove listens to this—“that
people who will oppose this move will th ink before commenting. The Commissioners,
in a few short years, have achieved more than  the old failed council  ever did. I recall a
shrill tone at the time, but every prediction of doom has not eventuated.” Irrigation New

items.speaker: Zealand has said
items.text: “Rural communities now have more opportunities to be involved in
water management through the collaborati ve approach of the Canterbury Water
Management Strategy. We are starting to see real gains through the zone committee and
we don’t want to go back to the nightmare  situation that rate payers suffered under
previously.”
Finally, Ng āi Tahu, representing tangata whenua and iwi, say: “ECan has a
significant role in issues of importance to Ng āi Tahu and the overall environmental
health of Canterbury’s land and water based economy … In our view the commissioners
7814 Env. Canterbury (Temp. Commissioners etc.) Amdt Bill 13 Feb 2013
have done a good job to date in addressing some very challenging issues. Iwi and
community participation in the Canterbury Water Management Strategy forums has
been a very worthwhile ex ercise.” So I know, Mr Cosg rove, that local government,
representing democratically elected members, the rural community, and Ng āi Tahu all
support the commissioners. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: I take it this micr ophone is working? It
is. Well, that was an extraordinary speech. Nicky Wagner is obviously orbiting in a
stratosphere that no one else  is. She got up and said that  there is overwhelming support
for this bill, the Environment Canterbur y (Temporary Commissioners and Improved
Water Management) Amendment Bill, inhere nt within which is a massive broken
promise from the Government, but we will get to that in a minute. Nicky Wagner’s
defence of this bill and the evidence that she provided for her claim that Cantabrians
overwhelmingly support an abrogation, yet again, of their democratic right to have a say
in their regional local government was that Federated Farmers, wh ich is sort of the
National Party in gumboots, Ngāi Tahu, and a couple of others—in fact, I think that was
it—had said that this was a good thing. Yet what she failed—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Local Government New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Oh, Local Government New Zealand, of course—
highly representative, is Local  Government New Zealand, of  grassroots Cantabrians.
Federated Farmers—highly representative, overwhelmingly, of 350,000-plus grassroots
Cantabrians. But what she failed to acknow ledge, given that I think—was she on the
Local Government and Environment Committee? I think so.

items.text: She is it.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Oh, she is the select committee. She failed to
acknowledge a thing called submissions. People get to have their say directly before a
select committee through a thing called subm issions. If you look at the submissions,
there were 95 of them. How many were in support? Five. How many were opposed?
Ninety. Even Nicky Wagner and Gerry Brownl ee could probably do the math using all
their fingers and toes and work out the percentage on that. Five submissions out of 95
supported it, and 90 submissions out of 95 oppos ed it. So I say to Ms Wagner that that
is called evidence before her own select co mmittee, which, of course, she conveniently
failed to mention, apart from Federated Farmers, Local Government New Zealand, and
Ngāi Tahu.
I will tell you what this is about. This is about a ma ssive broken promise by this
Government. Nick Smith said in March 2010 : “whatever the circumstances, the next
regional council elections in Canterbury will take place no later than those scheduled for
late 2013. The explicit intent is for the comm issioners to withdraw and be replaced by
elected representatives as s oon as their task is achieve d and the present systematic
issues are resolved.” That was a cast-iron pr omise. I remember the debate. I remember
us providing warnings that this could be ro lled over yet again. But we were told by the
Government “No, no, no.”, that we were bei ng negative, that this was all about doing
the right thing, and that this was a cast-ir on, pop-riveted, vulcanised promise. Well, the
Government broke it. That member, Nicky Wa gner, broke it, and the best she can do
today is cobble together a number of untru ths to say that the overwhelming number of
people in Canterbury and overwhelming numb ers of Cantabrians s upport the bill. Well,
that is piffle—absolute piffle.  If you look at what business people have said and if you
look at what grassroots community members have  said, that is total piffle. I say this to

items.speaker: Ms Wagner
items.text: people in Canterbury, where I live and other colleagues live, have had a bit
of a gutsful of being steamrolled by this Government, whether it be by, of course, Gerry
Brownlee’s promises around the earthquake ; Gerry Brownlee’s “my way or the
highway” sort of blunderbuss, steamroller management style around the earthquake; or
13 Feb 2013 Env. Canterbury (Temp. Commissioners etc.) Amdt Bill 7815
his promise about things like if you make impr ovements to your house, that will be part
of the deal—a broken promise. They have had a bit of a gutsful of being told what to
think, what to say, and how to act, and being told to shut up and take the medicine.
Actually, people in Christchurch and Great er Canterbury would like to have some
say—like to have some say—a nd make a contribution to their own future. But this
Government, of course, says that it knows best . It is interesting, because in the select
committee report—have a look at it—the Chief Human Rights Co mmissioner, David
Rutherford, said this: “The Commissi on considers that no good reason has been
provided for extending the present legislati on. The lack of public consultation about
content—or the continuing need for the le gislation—is an abuse of the democratic
process and does not reflect the real needs of Cantabrians … In our view the present
legislation has the potential to further exace rbate the resentment that has arisen in
Canterbury as a result”—these are very inte resting words for the Chief Human Rights
Commissioner to use—“of autocratic decisi on making.” That is what the Chief Human
Rights Commissioner says.
Then we get, of course, to the regulatory impact statement. The Government ignored
the regulatory impact statement. We know th at the Department of Internal Affairs’
advisers and the Ministry for the Envi ronment’s advisers recommended option one,
which was legislation to establish a tran sitional mixed governing body for Environment
Canterbury, with the provisi on for the Minister of Lo cal Government to review
arrangements by 2017. The Government rejected that. It absolutely rejected that. The
regulatory impact statement, of course, went on  to say this—it made three points; I will
read this one—“The extension of the Co mmissioners’ terms would continue to deny
Canterbury residents th e opportunity to vote for repres entatives on ECan. Also, given
the progress made by the Commissioners, there is no apparent reason for continuing this
level of intervention, which was used in response to ECan’s previous serious and
systemic dysfunction.” That is what the regula tory impact statement said, that is what
the Government’s own advisers said, and it rejected that advice.
So what have we got stacking up? We ha ve got 90 out of 95 submitters saying that
they oppose this bill. We have  got the vast majority of Cantabrians—apart from the
Government’s Federated Farmers mates—sayi ng that they oppose it. We have got the
Government’s own official advisers—the Department of Internal Affairs and the
Ministry for the Environment—recommending a transitional provision and a different
course of action leading to  democratic processes. A nd we also have the actual
regulatory impact statement sayi ng that this is undemocratic, that it is autocratic, and
that it is wrong. Of course, to cap it all o ff, as Nicky Wagner hides behind her desk, we
had one of the biggest broken promises ar ticulated in this Parliament—in this
Parliament. Why is it that Ms Wagner, the me mber for Christchurch Central, does not
trust her own community to be part of d ecision-making processes? Maybe, like Gerry
Brownlee, she fears this fact, that the community may stand up and say: “We do not
agree. We believe, Government, that you are wrong, and we want a di fferent course of
action.” I suspect that that is why these pe ople do not want Cantabrians to have a say.
They do not want to listen to any alternative advice.
We had Bill English before the select committee—sorry, we had the manufacturing
inquiry, I digress slightly, on Monday. I asked the former president of the
Manufacturers and Exporters Association whether he had had engagement with
Minister Joyce, the Minister for Economic  Development. No, none—zero since he took
the portfolio. The association has offered to speak and offered to meet, and the Minister
does not want to know. That is yet another example of this Government taking advice
from everybody else that suits its purpose, taking advice from yes-people.
7816 Env. Canterbury (Temp. Commissioners etc.) Amdt Bill 13 Feb 2013
Even if you look at economic policy, the IMF, the Reserve Bank, and Treasury all
say that we are heading for the rocks in re spect of the deficit,  but Bill English, of
course, says that he knows better than everyone else, including, we found out today, the
Westpac bank. This Government takes advice from those who will doff their hat, tug
their forelock, and say: “Yes, we agree.” I wo rry that even in our Public Service, the
days are gone of public serv ants being allowed to give free and frank advice without
fear or favour, such that they can say to a Minister: “Minister, we believe that your
course of action is wrong, but  we are professionals. If you deem it appropr iate to go
down that path, even though we think it w on’t work, we will implement it for you
because we are a professional Public Service. ” That is appropriate advice, to say: “We
think you’re wrong but will do what we’re told because you are the elected
Government.” I fear that, lik e this legislation, this G overnment has dumbed down our
Public Service to the point where it has just given up. There is no point in saying that
something will not work—whether it be charter schools, whether it be the student ratios,
whether it be this bill, or whether it be the school closures in Christchurch—the
Government is going to do it anyway; it will not listen to the advice.
